item.title: This mini PC with a 5.7-inch touchscreen drops to $480
item.itunes:title: This mini PC with a 5.7-inch touchscreen drops to $480
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Mini PCs are versatile, compact computers you can buy on a budget. They can replace traditional desktops and also become a valuable part of a home lab or smart home. The only downside is that you have to buy everything else, like a monitor, keyboard, and mouse.

But that's not the case with this AE86 model, which features a 5.7-inch screen, touchpad, mouse, and keyboard. The $600 price tag seems fair, but we really like the $120 Amazon coupon that drops it to $480.

AE86 5.7" Mini PC
CPU
Intel N95
Memory
16GB DDR4 RAM
Storage
512GB SSD
Display
5.7-inch touchscreen
See at Amazon

The best of both worlds

Credit: AE86

I love a good mini PC. However, I don't like how cluttered things can get when you add all the required accessories. This device, the AE86, brings the best of both worlds: a small form factor with a screen, keyboard, and mouse.

To be clear, you're not going to be banging out 1000s of words on this device, but just having everything in one place is going to add some convenience when it's needed. The 5.7-inch screen also supports touch input, making interaction easier.

As for the other specifications, you're looking at an Intel N95 CPU, 16GB of DDR4 RAM, and 512GB of SSD storage. It also has a front-facing camera and two USB-C ports, HDMI, DisplayPort, two USB-A ports, and an Ethernet port.

If you want, you can use it as a home PC and connect up to three monitors. It also has Bluetooth 5.2 and Wi-Fi 6, along with dual speakers and a microphone. It comes with Windows 11 and Office 2024 preinstalled. You can install Linux if you want to.

While it doesn't say how long the 2,150mAh battery will last, we can't imagine it lasting more than 5 hours. It'll depend on how you use it, but it's still nice to remove it from power and still get some functionality.

Just be sure to clip the $120 off coupon before you check out in order to get the best price.

item.title: I was ready to pay for a remote desktop app, but Windows 11 already ships one for free
item.itunes:title: I was ready to pay for a remote desktop app, but Windows 11 already ships one for free
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For every AI feature of questionable utility that Microsoft advertises relentlessly, there's a useful one hiding in the OS in plain sight. Many of these tools aid productivity or everyday troubleshooting, and some let you forgo paying for utilities that do the same job outright.

Quick Assist is one of such useful features that comes pre-installed on Windows 11 Home and Pro. It connects to Windows 10 machines, and the only setup you need to use it is a Microsoft account on the helper's end. The person on the other side only needs a six-digit code. Here's why I think Microsoft should be talking about it more instead of letting users discover it by accident.

What is Quick Assist on Windows 11?

And what can you do with it?

Quick Assist is Microsoft's built-in app for sharing a Windows device with someone else over a remote connection, and it allows them to view the screen, annotate it, and even assume full control for complex troubleshooting tasks.

As you'd expect, it's popular amongst IT support technicians, but there's nothing keeping regular users on the OS from using it, provided they're on Windows 11 or Windows 10. Since Windows 11 version 22H2, it has been pre-installed on Windows machines, and Windows 10 users can get it from the Microsoft Store.

Besides the app itself, what the helper would need to use this feature is a Microsoft account. The one sharing their desktop doesn't need to sign in to any account at all, and just needs internet access. The connection itself runs over the Remote Desktop Protocol and is encrypted with TLS 1.2. In case you were wondering, Microsoft can't access the session or see actions or keystrokes, neither does retain data about either the host or the helper for longer than three days, as per their documentation.

6 Windows features aimed at accessibility you didn't know everyone should use

Anyone can benefit from accessibility features

1
By  Anurag Singh

How does Quick Assist work?

And what devices are supported?

Starting a Quick Assist session is as straightforward as it gets, and I'd even argue that it's the simplest way to share your desktop with another user. You can simply search for "Quick Assist" on Search or use the combination Ctrl + Win + Q to launch the app.

The next step depends on whether you're the one doing the helping or are being helped. The person doing the helping clicks "Help someone" on the app to generate a time-limited six-digit code, which they pass on by phone or by message.

The person on the other end, then, has to type in the code and allow screen sharing before anything shows up on the helper's screen. Once that's done, there's all there is to it. The helper can request control, and the sharer gets another prompt to either allow or deny. Nothing happens without the sharer's consent, and they can pull control back any time with "Cancel control." In the session, the helper also gets access to a few useful tools like a pointer, annotation tools, and a chat window for typed messages.

On the device front, Quick Assist works on both Windows 11 and Windows 10 as I mentioned, but what's interesting is that the two can talk to each other in either direction. This means the helper and the sharer can be on either versions of Windows and the app will still work the same, which I find useful, because for this reason, I've been able to help out my sister who for some reason just refuses to get Windows 11 on her laptop, and keeps running into an issue or another due to the fact.

Besides the obvious documented use-case, there's nothing stopping you from sharing one of your device's desktop with another as well. For example, I can use my laptop to access my desktop in the other room by entering the six-digit code once, and it functions just like a remote desktop app that way.

5 Windows networking features you should consider using

Windows has a ton of advanced networking features that can make your life easier

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

But Windows comes with many other useful remote tools, too

There are many use-cases for them, and they come for free on your OS

While Quick Assist handles the "help a friend" use-case, I've used it to double as a makeshift remote desktop between my own computers. For anything more involved, Windows also offers two other tools that do the job bettter, and both of them save you money otherwise spent on a third-party app.

Remote Desktop would be the one that most people would have heard of, and unlike Quick Assist, it's purpose-built for connecting to your own machines. The only catch is that it's limited to Windows 11 Pro and higher editions when it comes to hosting an RDP session, so if you want to reach your gaming PC from a laptop or jump into a Windows VM in Hyper-V, the host needs to be on Pro edition. The client side, however, works on any edition, so a Home machine can connect to a Pro host, just not the other way round.

Then, there's Windows Remote Assistant (msra.exe), which is the legacy option that predates Quick Assist by over a decade. The one real advantage it offers is that neither party needs a Microsoft account to use it. You can launch it from Run, send an invitation file, and the person on the other end can just connect with a password you've set.

These are the tools I want Microsoft to boast about, not Copilot

Remote desktop utilities are dime-a-dozen on third-party app stores and online, but for most simple troubleshooting tasks or accessing one PC's desktop from the other, Windows' built-in utilities can do the job just fine, and Quick Assist, alongside the rest of Windows remote tools, come with your OS for free. Even if your workflow rarely requires it, it's always good to know that you've got native options on your PC sitting just one click away.

item.title: I used Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra to build the same portfolio — the difference was immediately obvious
item.itunes:title: I used Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra to build the same portfolio — the difference was immediately obvious
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Two of the biggest model launches this year happened just days apart, and since then the entire internet has run test after test on them. Naturally, my feed was inundated by all the utilities and designs that people were vibe-coding with Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, especially when it came to comparing them. I must say, it's been difficult picking my favorites because taste is mainly subjective. So I wanted to put them to the test myself and see how they actually follow instructions and improvise on the spot.

A personal portfolio seemed like a pretty fair test. It's something I've been toying with for a while but haven't fully got to yet, so this would be the perfect head-start to get the ball rolling. I gave both the same prompt, and the one that not only gave me the best result but was also the best behaved will be getting the job of helping me finish my portfolio.

I used Claude Code, Antigravity, and Perplexity Computer to build a portfolio — there was a clear winner

The results were surprising.

27
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Two flagships, two days apart

Everyone had an opinion on which one designs better, so I gave them the same job

Claude Fable 5.1 came out on September 1, with GPT-6 Astra following two days later. Fable 5.1 is Anthropic's most capable public model, built on the same underlying model as the restricted Mythos 5.1 but with extra safeguards so regular users can use it. Astra is OpenAI's first GPT-6 model, and OpenAI says it has better visual judgment when it builds websites and apps.

Both cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output on the API. But inside the apps is a different story. On Claude Pro, Fable runs on paid usage credits, which is how I paid for mine, while Astra is included with ChatGPT Plus but draws from the shared Work and Codex allowance (anywhere between 5-45 messages every five hours by OpenAI's estimate).

I ran both on Medium effort - this is my favorite reasoning level because it's not as slow or expensive as high/extra, but still produces better results than low. I also ran both in the desktop GUIs. This choice was a no-brainer; both have a browser preview and can actually see their own work, plus it's a lot more interactive than the terminal, which is just better for iteration.

The prompt covered who I am and what tools I used, with a few style rules, such as keeping all the text lowercase. I gave it a list of projects to choose from and left some of the projects themselves open on purpose, plus an extra section of each model's choosing, because how they filled these blanks was what I wanted to see.

I gave Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6, and Grok 4.6 a complex design challenge and one clearly won

Only one built production-ready code.

2
By  Parth Shah

Fable 5.1 in Claude Code

It took its time, then went back and checked its own work

Fable opened my portfolio with "i write about tech, then make it move," and the bio underneath just says "the work is below. that's the whole bio." This is perhaps a bit too cheeky for my taste, but I did ask for a minimal bio, after all. I guess Fable took it quite literally.

For the project writeups, I kept the details light on purpose because I wanted to test how much the models could infer from the prompt. Fable filled in the rest by framing every piece around the story behind it. For example, in my keyboard post it wrote a line about shooting it with a borrowed macro lens, which I never told it, but it could have inferred from the image files I gave it. The vertical shorts were described as cut on a phone in Alight Motion within an hour of a tech story breaking - they weren't tech news stories specifically, but news stories I turned into short motion graphics nonetheless.

Visually, it kept the page very balanced. In motion graphics, contrast creates focus, but it needs a balance or it will just create janky, jittery chaos. And I feel like Fable nailed this with both the stills and the animation. The page was dark with a lot of color, but the colors were subdued and perfectly matched the undertones of the background. Hovering over a project or tool card lifted the card slightly with a soft glow. Each tool card got its own animation tied to the actual app, for example, Figma has shapes, text, and a cursor that moves into place when you hover.

Furthermore, opening a project card brings up a timeline scrubber with acts and a running timecode, so the detail view is basically an editing timeline. It also added a "field notes" section on its own, with lines like "if the viewer notices the easing, it's too much easing".

After the build, it screenshotted its own pages in Claude Code's browser, then it kept working and caught little issues like lines overlapping. So it checked its own work without me having to ask.

I replaced Adobe, Figma, and Canva with ChatGPT and one open-source tool

Girl math says this counts as three cancelled subscriptions

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

GPT-6 Astra in Codex

Five minutes, a clear direction, and a lot of color

Astra was done in about half the time Fable took, and it even told me its plan before getting started. The Codex side of the ChatGPT app is nice to work in, too. Every diff shows up in a changes panel next to the chat, and there's an Annotate button in the preview for marking up the page. It also checked keyboard navigation and reduced-motion support without being asked, which Fable didn't bring up.

The portfolio hero says "good stories. strange motion." in huge type, with an acid yellow asterisk off to one side. It's confident and very polished, I can definitely see what it was going for. The write-ups for my projects went more abstract, though. Astra called them "selected experiments" and leaned a lot on big concept-film themes to describe them. This was perhaps a little over the top for my taste.

Every project got a big full-bleed cover in its own saturated color with very sharp edges, and one is pretty much an orange sunburst poster with "look again" across it. This is a lot bolder than I'd hoped for - they're visually appealing on their own, but four in a row just creates too much business for me, it almost reads like a magazine. Hover motion was also there, but it felt underwhelming next to Fable's, almost like the movement was linear instead of a Bézier curve.

The detail view had a nicer structure with sections like "the question" and "behind the frames", plus a scrubber called "your turn to edit" that morphs a soft shape into a resolved one. Its extra section was a tiny motion lab with orbit, scatter, and breathe buttons - this was the most playful bit either of the models built, which I do appreciate.

I asked Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT to build a customer landing page, and only one nailed the brief

Only one is most likely not to lose me any customers

6
By  Abhinav Raj

The loudest page isn't always the one you remember

At the end of the day, it just comes down to personal taste. Astra did a good job and it would make for a good magazine spread, but I feel like it tried a little too hard to be bold and captivating. Everything on the page competed for my attention at the same volume, whereas Fable's creation had more dips and peaks that held my focus. Fable also understood the context of who I am and my projects a little better.

I’ll probably end up using Fable’s codebase as the starting point for my actual portfolio, though it’ll need a fair bit of tweaking and proper project details before I publish anything.

item.title: I gave my TV a free speed boost by changing these 4 settings
item.itunes:title: I gave my TV a free speed boost by changing these 4 settings
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If your older (or brand new) smart TV starts to feel slow, you might think it is time to buy a new one. However, you can do a few simple things in the settings menu to perk it up. It had been a few years since I'd really dug into my main TV's settings menu, and I got it feeling new again. Plus, I didn't have to exhaustively search for the right code to access the factory service menu to make tweaks.

You can boost your TV's responsiveness with a few changes in the regular settings menu you may have overlooked. If your smart TV is starting to feel sluggish, try adjusting these settings to speed it up.

Update your TV's software

It doesn't always update in the background

One of the first places I look on smart TVs when the performance isn't optimal is the software updates section. Your TV is like a computer or your phone and needs software updates. TV manufacturers often release updates that fix bugs and improve performance and security. However, not all models download updates automatically, especially older TVs.

Go to the Settings menu and find the section that lets you manually check for updates. If you can't find it, it is usually under the About or Preferences menu, or it has a clearly labeled Update Software option. While you're there, see if you can set it to check for updates automatically. Also, check the menu for a firmware update option. I updated an older TV's firmware for a relative, and it made the old set feel a generation newer and added new features.

This simple trick fixed my laggy smart TV

If your smart TV's operating system is stuttering, clearing its cache is often a quick way to speed it up.

2
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Clear app cache

It builds up over time and slows down the TV

Most people don't think of their TV as a computer, but it actually is. It has an operating system, processor, and RAM to run the apps. After switching between apps and using them often, the cache of temporary data can become bloated and corrupt, slowing the TV down. Like clearing the cache on your PC, clearing the cache on your TV can also make it feel faster.

Most smart TVs have a dedicated option to clear the cache in the Settings menu, including Roku and Fire TVs. In your TV's settings menu, go to the Apps section, select your most used apps, and choose the Clear Cache, Clear App Caches, or Clear Data button. I've done this on many of my smart TVs, and it often improves UI responsiveness and app load time.

Disable ACR

It lets manufacturers track your viewing

Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) lets TV manufacturers monitor your viewing habits. They use and share that data with third parties to target ads and content through the interface. It monitors app usage and program-viewing habits. It doesn't just monitor what you watch on the TV itself, but also on all devices connected to other input ports. It can even see what you are watching via an OTA antenna and self-hosted media platforms like Plex and Jellyfin.

Turning it off will help improve your privacy. It can also improve performance by reducing background data processing and network traffic. That frees up the set's resources for better performance from the TV's operating system and the apps you want to run smoothly on your screen.

Disabling ACR varies between sets and is buried in the menu system. But you'll often find it in the Privacy, Apps, About, or Personalization section of the settings menu. Once it's off, you can rest easy knowing you have a modicum of privacy while watching TV at home. Keep in mind it doesn't block all usage data, metrics, and analytics. For that, you'd need to run a Pi-hole.

Restart your TV

It never completely powers down

It sounds simple, right? Turn it off every night. However, when you turn off your smart TV with the remote's power button, it enters a low-power state so it can resume quickly and pick up where you left off. It's like Sleep mode on a PC, so the television never completely reboots. Occasionally, rebooting your TV clears temporary files in memory and resets inputs, which can fix glitches that happen after it runs for a long time.

It's like restarting your phone or computer when it is acting up or running slow. It can fix a sluggish menu system and frozen apps, and it refreshes the TV. Since I work with several streaming devices, I reboot my work TVs a lot, but I'm not so good at regularly restarting my personal televisions.

When the TV runs slowly, a thorough reboot can cure it and is a good starting point for troubleshooting. Sets vary, but the restart option is typically in the power section of the settings menu. Also, while in the power section, disable energy-saving mode to preserve your display and improve picture vibrancy and brightness.

4 hidden LG TV settings I changed immediately to make my new TV even better

A TV is better when it's just a TV

By  João Carrasqueira

Breathing new life into a smart TV

You can make a smart TV run faster by adjusting menu settings. From turning off picture settings like motion smoothing (or TruMotion, Action Smoothing, or something else depending on the brand) to simply remembering to reboot your TV properly. Think of it like improving your computer's performance: updating, uninstalling unused apps, disabling animations, and tweaking other settings to speed it up.

item.title: 4 Google apps I replace on every new Android phone, and every replacement is free
item.itunes:title: 4 Google apps I replace on every new Android phone, and every replacement is free
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Getting a new Android phone usually means spending the first hour removing apps I don't want and setting up the ones I actually use. Over time, I stopped treating this as something I had to figure out every time. I now have a small list of replacements that I install almost automatically whenever I switch phones. They cover some of the apps I use most often, and I don't have to pay for any of them. More importantly, I didn't pick these replacements just to be different. Each one solves a specific problem I had with the default experience and fits better into the way I use Android.

Google Chrome replaced with Firefox

Firefox gives me more control

Chrome is usually the first browser I see on a new Android phone, but it is also one of the first apps I replace. I switched to Firefox because I prefer having more control over how I browse, especially on my phone. It gives me a familiar browsing experience without locking me into the default Android setup.

What I like most is how Firefox handles customization. I can change the way the browser behaves, organize my frequently visited sites, and use extensions that aren't available in Chrome's Android version. That makes a noticeable difference when I use my phone for more than just casual web browsing.

Firefox also fits nicely into my existing workflow because I already use it on my desktop. My browsing experience feels more consistent across devices, rather than requiring two separate setups.

I don't claim that Firefox is perfect, and Chrome still has its advantages. But for my everyday browsing, Firefox gives me enough flexibility to make the switch worthwhile. Since it's free, replacing Chrome costs me nothing beyond a few minutes of setup.

Google Keep replaced with Joplin

Joplin gives my notes more structure

I used Google Keep for years because it makes capturing quick thoughts incredibly easy. But as my notes started growing, I wanted something that could handle more than short reminders and random ideas. That’s when I moved to Joplin.

What I like about Joplin is that it feels more like a proper note-taking system. I can organize notes into notebooks, use tags, write in Markdown, and keep longer pieces of information without the interface getting in my way. I also find it easier to separate personal notes, research, and things I want to refer to later.

The Markdown support is particularly useful for me. I often write notes while researching something, and having proper formatting makes those notes much easier to work with later. Attachments are also handy when I need to keep supporting files with a note.

Keep is still perfectly fine for quick lists and reminders, but Joplin fits my workflow better. It is free to use, gives me more control over my notes, and doesn't feel like I’ll outgrow it as quickly.

6 forgotten open-source apps that survived every productivity trend by keeping things simple

These old-school apps simply kept doing their jobs.

10
By  Yash Patel

Google Files replaced with Material Files

A cleaner way to manage files

I replaced Google Files almost immediately. I prefer having a file manager that gives me a clear view of what is stored on my phone without adding too much around it. My replacement is Material Files, a free and open-source file manager that keeps things simple.

The interface is one of the main reasons I stick with it. I can quickly browse folders, move or copy files, rename items, and manage different storage locations without digging through layers of menus. It also supports common archive formats, which come in handy when I need to quickly open or create a ZIP file from my phone.

I particularly like the dual-pane layout when working with files. It makes moving things between folders much easier than constantly going back and forth between locations. The app also feels responsive, so basic file operations don't become a chore.

Google Files does more than I need from a file manager, while Material Files stays focused on the basics. Since it is free and doesn't cost me anything to switch, I install it as part of my usual setup on a new Android phone.

Google Photos replaced with Immich

item.title: Used enterprise hard drives are the last real storage deal, and I trust them more than new ones
item.itunes:title: Used enterprise hard drives are the last real storage deal, and I trust them more than new ones
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The case made against used hard drives is similar to all other kinds of pre-owned hardware, but it rings truer because of the moving parts inside. You’re putting your data on something that has already spent years spinning in a chassis you’ve never seen, so some hesitation is definitely natural, but I think we have the risk backwards. A used enterprise drive tells you what it is and where it’s been, while a new consumer drive tells you nothing until it fails. Add what’s happened to storage prices across the board, and secondhand enterprise drives are the last real deal in storage and the ones I’d rather own.

I built a NAS with enterprise SAS drives, and the hidden costs nearly matched new SATA drives

SAS is a standard that comes with its own unique pitfalls

By  Ty Sherback

New drives got expensive, and used ones only partly followed suit

Prices went up for pre-owned enterprise storage, but by as much as new storage did

The hard drive market stopped prioritizing home buyers somewhere in the last year. Western Digital’s CEO told investors in January that the company was essentially sold out for calendar 2026, with supply agreements already reaching into the following two years, and Seagate has described similar commitments. Prices followed suit with this sentiment, and some consumers were priced out of higher-capacity storage.

Used enterprise storage sits further downstream from that, and while it hasn't been complete immune to price increases because of the overall increase in demand, its supply comes from a different place entirely. These drives are pulled from servers that have been decomissioned or the drives themselves have reached that data center's quota for wear and tear. Resellers get these drives as manufacturer recertified in many cases, but sometimes they'll refurbish them for sale on their own. That stock tends to sit a tier or two below the current flagship capacities, which is where home NAS users shop anyway.

If you're willing to go the SAS route, your pool of potential storage options widens further, but with some asterisks. I happen to have two used enterprise SAS drives in my home lab, running off of an LSI 9207-8i HBA card. Running one of those cards is a hard requirement if you're using a consumer motherboard as a foundation like I am. Add in the cost of the cables and extra power draw, and some of the savings disappear up front, but you can also add more drives without paying that cost again, since a SAS HBA can handle many drives on it at the same time.

4 things you should know before shucking external hard drives for your NAS

Shucking can prove useful to save money, but watch out for these points.

3
By  Rich Edmonds

I know what I got myself into

These drives have a known history, and sometimes that's better than no history

A used enterprise drive is an open book and can tell you things about it that a brand-new consumer drive simply can't, so long as you get it from a reputable source.

Seagate rates the Exos 7E8s in my system for 550TB of workload a year and a two-million-hour MTBF, and its own datasheet puts that workload at ten times what a desktop drive is built for. Mainstream NAS drives like the IronWolf and WD Red are rated for 180TB, and while my pool will probably never reach either number, having that extra breathing room is important. I'm living well within the confines of the drive's limits, despite the fact that they've been pre-owned. The 7E8 also uses conventional magnetic recording, a detail that once upon a time, wasn't so easy to find on a spec sheet. Western Digital admitted in 2020 that some WD Red models had shipped with undisclosed shingled recording, which is suboptimal for the exact kind of use that they were sold for.

The second-biggest thing is the drive's history, which is easily checked with a SMART scan. One of my drives arrived with roughly 2,700 power-on hours and the other with about 3,100, which is still well within the limits for this drive. One had been power-cycled a couple of thousand times and the other a few dozen, and neither has a grown defect or an uncorrected error on its record.

I finally set up TrueNAS cloud sync for the first time, and it blew my mind

TrueNAS taught me more than I ever wanted to know about storage

8
By  Nolen Jonker

Used drives don't necessarily fail less

It's more of a timing phenomenon

Enterprise customers buy brand-new enterprise drives, not used ones. That sounds like a really obvious statement, but when drive failures follow a bathtub curve, with most failures happening in a drives infancy or late in its life cycle, there's always going to be some percentage of drives that fail early in any given batch.

That doesn't mean that recertified drives fail less often than brand-new ones, and it also doesn't take into account things like warranty coverage, which is always going to be better with new drives.

5 HDD myths that you shouldn't believe

HDDs might be on their way out, but these myths are still alive

4
By  Tanveer Singh

Buy from a reputable seller, and you should be fine

Recertified enterprise drives are pretty reliable

Used enterprise storage is way more sketchy if purchased from a seller with no track record. Random eBay sellers with no history are way more likely to be selling you a drive that has had its SMART data scrubbed away, so picking and choosing who you buy from is just as important as the make and model.

One of the most popular spots for home lab enthusiasts and NAS-enjoyers is ServerPartDeals, who take decommissioned hardware, recertify/refurbish it if the manufacturer didn't, and then sell it at a discount. It's where I've bought all of my pre-owned storage personally, and they're held in pretty high regard in home storage circles. There are multiple eBay sellers that have hundreds (or thousands) of positive reviews doing exactly the same thing, though I can't personally vouch for them.

I ordered refurbished HDDs for my NAS - are they really that bad?

While I wouldn't use them to store essential files, refurbished drives are somewhat useful in cost-effective file-sharing servers

11
By  Ayush Pande

Used enterprise storage is still an unlock despite the price increases

If your storage plan is a two-bay Synology box and no backup, none of this applies, and you should buy new with the longest warranty you can afford. If you’re willing to add redundancy, keep a backup, and read a SMART report, the used enterprise market is still the best value in storage. It just won’t stay that way forever.

item.title: I handed a worst-case scenario to Intel's cut-down iGPU, and its gaming performance still surprised me
item.itunes:title: I handed a worst-case scenario to Intel's cut-down iGPU, and its gaming performance still surprised me
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Integrated graphics are usually an afterthought, especially on a mini PC that's decked out for home lab use. The Minisforum box I have and its Intel Core Ultra 9 389H aren't particularly adept at gaming, but when trying a handful of titles on it, new and old, it surprised me. It has a cut-down version of the integrated graphics in the full-fat chip, featuring only a third of the Xe3 cores. It also only has one stick of DDR5 SODIMM memory, which is about as bad of configuration as you can give an integrated GPU. Despite that, it ran most of what I threw at it.

AMD's X3D CPUs only help with two things, and most gamers have neither

3D V-Cache isn't a reason to buy blindly.

11
By  Hamlin Rozario

The 386H gets the smaller version of Intel's Xe3 graphics

It's not the full graphics package

Intel's Panther Lake chips come with two very different tiers of integrated graphics. The Core Ultra X parts carry the Arc B390 with 12 Xe3 cores, and that's the one behind most of the gaming coverage. The Core Ultra 9 386H in the MS-03 mini PC I have isn't an X chip. It uses the same Xe3 architecture with only four of those cores, so it's significantly cut down compared to the main version.

I tested a handful of games on Windows 11 with the performance BIOS profile and mostly at 1080p to give this thing a fighting chance. The main thing working against this particular box is that it's limited to one stick of SODIMM DDR5, which doesn't only severely hamper memory performance, but also puts more strain on the iGPU, since it relies on system memory for VRAM.

Integrated graphics are no longer a compromise — modern iGPUs match last-gen discrete cards and cost nothing extra

The graphics chip already inside your processor is far better than you think.

3
By  Jasmine Mannan

Older games ran comfortably

A solid average framerate

Black Mesa was the first thing I tried. It's the 2020 remake of Half-Life, built on Valve's Source engine, and at native 1080p on low settings it averaged around 70 FPS. That's not a demanding game, but it's a full 3D shooter running at native resolution with no upscaling.

GTA IV was more interesting. The 2008 PC port has a long-standing reputation for running badly on hardware that should handle it easily, so it's a useful test of whether a system has headroom to waste. On low settings it averaged about 100 FPS at 1080p and about 60 FPS at 1440p. The frame rate fell roughly in step with the extra pixels, which suggests the graphics side was the limit at those settings and not the CPU. Either way, 60 FPS at 1440p from four Xe3 cores is more than I expected, especially for a game like this.

I pushed FSR 4.1 and DLSS 4.5 to their limits on older hardware, and one changed my mind about 4K gaming

It was neck-and-neck, until it wasn't

6
By  Samarveer Singh

GTA V Enhanced was a pleasant surprise

More than playable on a box of this size is impressive

GTA V Enhanced is the 2025 PC update that brought over the ray tracing features from the current console versions, and Rockstar's minimum spec asks for a dedicated card with 4GB of VRAM. I ran it on the game's minimum preset at 1080p, and it averaged around 90 FPS through the opening sequence.

This is, of course, with the caveat that gameplay within Los Santos could suffer a little more, but even so, the game could lose a third of its framerate and still be at a very playable 60 FPS. For integrated graphics running on one stick of RAM, that's a strong result.

We tested it: iGPUs are good, actually

The integrated graphics in your laptop has a lot more power than you give it credit for.

4
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A recent triple-A title is asking too much

Battlefield 6 is well optimized, but this is asking too much of the 386H and its iGPU

I decided to stretch my luck and try a more recent game. Battlefield 6 has been a mainstay in my library, so I decided to fire it up. It firmly pushed this box to its limit.

With XeSS set to ultra performance at 1080p, this thing averaged around 35 FPS in an online Domination lobby. On paper, that clears EA's minimum spec of 30 FPS at 1080p for a dedicated card with 6GB of VRAM, but that's at native rendering. XeSS ultra performance renders at a third of the output resolution on each axis, so the game was drawing a 640 by 360 image and scaling it up. That's a ninth of the pixels, and there isn't much image left to work with at that point. On my 32" 4K OLED, the game looked like a shambles. It was somewhat playable, but not what I would consider a great experience. Vehicle combat might not be too bad, but infantry stuff is off the table here.

4 tweaks I always make to get more performance from my Windows 11 gaming handheld

I aim to strike a balance between how good a game looks and its frame rate.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

One stick of RAM means these numbers are the floor

Adding another stick would boost performance significantly

Since iGPUs rely on system memory for VRAM, it's no surprise that this configuration suffers specifically in BF6. The minimum requirements call for dual-channel memory, and that's with a dGPU. With one stick installed, the MS-03 is running single-channel, which gives the iGPU roughly half the theoretical memory bandwidth it would have with two. If you were to add a second stick to his configuration, you'd see a significant boost in performance in all games.

4 ways you can use dual GPU setups in your normal PC

Assuming you're able to grab two graphics cards in this economy

7
By  Ayush Pande

Panther Lake's worst iGPU in a bad setup is still decent

Even though it's suffering with single-channel RAM, the iGPU in this Core Ultra 9 386H is impressive. I'm surprised that it was able to push such playable framerates in a title like GTA V Enhanced, though it's no surprise why it falls short in Battlefield 6. For older titles, even those that are triple-A, integrated graphics has become surprisingly good.

item.title: I used only local AI for a week and learned what actually needs the cloud
item.itunes:title: I used only local AI for a week and learned what actually needs the cloud
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have been relying on cloud-based AI tools for almost everything lately. While tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are capable, I started wondering how much of my workflow I could move to local LLMs.

I replaced my usual cloud-based assistants with local alternatives, put them through real-world tasks, and found where offline AI shines and where the cloud still has a clear advantage.

Trying to self-host LLMs made me realize local AI has a friction problem, not a quality problem

Think of it as the Linux desktop problem, all over again

30
By  Samarveer Singh

Getting started was easier than expected

Local LLMs shine in many areas

I expected setting up local AI to be a complicated process, but tools like LM Studio and Ollama made it straightforward. I downloaded a few popular models, including Qwen and Gemma, and had them running on my computer in no time.

What impressed me most was how capable they were at everyday tasks. I could brainstorm article ideas, generate outlines, rewrite awkward paragraphs, summarize short documents, create a robust diet plan, and even get help with basic coding questions.

The responses were quick, and I didn’t have to worry about sending my prescription to a remote server. For these simple tasks, I rarely felt the need to open ChatGPT or Claude.

Coding was the real challenge

Simple scripts are only the beginning

Coding was one area where I wanted local AI to succeed. I tried Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, a relatively lightweight yet capable coding model that I could run through LM Studio. To my surprise, it handled basic and moderately complex tasks quite well.

I could generate Python scripts, fix straightforward bugs, explain unfamiliar code, and even make changes to smaller projects without much trouble; however, things started falling apart when I pushed it further.

Tasks involving multiple files, complicated debugging, and larger codebases often required repeated prompts and manual intervention. This is where I started missing Claude Code. Its ability to understand an entire project, navigate files, plan changes, and tackle complicated problems.

These are difficult to replicate with a small local model. Local AI is perfectly usable for quick coding assistance, but I won’t replace my cloud-based coding tools just yet.

Research exposed the biggest limitations

Offline knowledge can only go so far

This was probably the biggest dealbreaker for me. I was recently shopping for an OLED monitor and couldn’t decide between the Samsung Smart Monitor M9 and the Odyssey OLED G8. I tried using my local LLM to compare them, but it was working with outdated information.

It had no idea about the latest Odyssey G8 model with an improved OLED panel and a USB-C port supporting up to 98W power delivery. That’s when I turned to ChatGPT, and the difference was immediately noticeable.

ChatGPT helped me compare the latest models, understand their differences, and narrow down my options based on my specific requirements. I wanted a monitor that would work seamlessly with my Windows desktop, MacBook Pro, and Fire TV Stick.

This is exactly where cloud-based AI with access to current information shines.

Local AI doesn’t work well with my everyday tools

Cloud integrations are hard to replace

Another area where local AI fell short was integrations with my everyday productivity apps. With ChatGPT, I can connect services like Notion, Outlook, Google Drive, and more to create a powerful productivity hub.

For instance, I can ask ChatGPT to create a database in Notion, summarize my latest emails, pull relevant documents from Drive, check pending tasks in Asana, and more.

Similarly, Gemini works well with Google services like Tasks, Keep Notes, YouTube Music, WhatsApp, Canva, and other services.

Replicating this convenience with local AI isn’t straightforward. It requires configuring APIs, setting up connectors, and building custom workflows. While it’s certainly possible, I don’t want to spend hours configuring integrations that already work seamlessly with ChatGPT.

My local LLM can call Claude when it's stuck, and it changed everything about my local-first setup

Local LLMs aren't very good on their own

14
By  Anurag Singh

Long documents tested my patience

I spent more time managing models than using them

Things became frustrating when I started working with lengthy documents. Summarizing a short PDF or extracting key points from a few pages was straightforward, but larger technical documents were a different story.

Depending on the model and context settings, responses became slower, important details were occasionally missed, and I had to break documents into small chunks.

With Gemini Notebooks or ChatGPT Projects, I can simply upload lengthy documents and start asking questions without worrying as much about the limitations.

Then there is the maintenance aspect. I spent a surprising amount of time downloading different models, experimenting with quantization levels, adjusting context windows, and monitoring RAM usage. Switching between models for writing, coding, and reasoning also became tedious.

A reality check for local AI

Local LLMs are quite capable for brainstorming ideas, rewriting paragraphs, summarizing short notes, and answering basic questions. However, the cracks started showing as soon as I pushed them to complex tasks.

My experiment also made me realize why I rely on cloud-based tools in the first place. There is something to be said about convenience. My last week with local AI taught me that it’s not really about choosing between local and cloud AI, but knowing when each one makes sense.

We tend to shelve old laptops, phones, and gadgets in a rarely visited desk drawer. The devices stay there collecting dust, never to be used again. New hardware replaces them, and it's sometimes sad to see the plight of what used to be absolutely great a while ago. But old devices have a redemption arc going on these days. Almost every computing device, small or big, can be repurposed into something useful.

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is quite old now and mostly unfit for demanding self-hosted tools. However, I was very impressed when I first bought it a couple of years back. It wasn’t a great fit for NextCloud or a media streaming server. So I turned it into a password manager server, and it's been quietly running without any major management.

A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W has many uses

Acting as a local password manager

Not all self-hosted tools need a ton of resources, and you can find some useful ones. Lately, I've switched to an Adobe Acrobat alternative called BentoPDF that works with very little memory. You might think it's less useful. But that's not the case with what self-hosted developers have been building recently. Similarly, OmniTools is a suite packed with nearly 100 tools for file, image, and video-related tasks. Similarly, there are a few self-hosted password manager options like Bitwarden and a few more.

Self-hosting Vaultwarden is the best decision I ever made, and migrating to it took 15 minutes

Vaultwarden truly is the best password manager out there

2
By  Ayush Pande

However, most of them will immediately rule out a low-powered device like the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. So I went with Vaultwarden, a Bitwarden-based password manager that runs locally and doesn't need much power. I was skeptical of its features, but it turned out to be exactly like a premium-tier tool. Vaultwarden made me jump ship from LastPass and save money on annual subscriptions. Additional perks of using it are keeping my data locally available, which gives me peace.

The original setup was minimalistic

DietPi made it possible

An SBC like the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W has 512MB of memory, and only 412MB is left after it takes some for the GPU. So, picking the right Raspberry Pi operating system is crucial. I couldn't go with a GUI OS because I needed to host it as a server with minimal interaction. Even heavy CLI options like Armbian were a no-go due to a lack of features. DietPi remains my no-nonsense pick after three years because it respects puny hardware.

On my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, the OS needs about 70MB to run, leaving plenty of room for other options. I installed it, and after a quick initial setup, I installed Vaultwarden via the DietPi-software utility. It's one of the numerous tools available with the OS, which makes it a compelling choice. Vaultwarden is a painless install and works without HTTPS due to the internal configuration of the OS.

For setup, I imported passwords from Chrome and a few other browsers. It creates a few vaults, and that's about it. After that, I peeked into the features, and it's the usual set you get with other similar tools. It includes a password generator, checker, and other related tools. You can use the Bitwarden browser extension, which enables autofill and a few other features. I also added Tailscale so I could access the server outside my home from a phone or laptop.

This setup worked for nearly ten months before I decided to make some changes to it. These two tools and the OS used about 150MB, and I saw potential in it. A containerized approach would improve it and use idle memory for other tools. I also ignored one roadblock that occurred because the tools weren't served over HTTPS.

Adding Docker and HTTPS support

Enabling app access

When I first created the Vaultwarden server, it worked over HTTP. But when I moved it to Docker, it stopped working without HTTPS. I also overlooked mobile app access, which forced me to use the web interface every time. The problem with that was the lack of an autofill feature while signing in to apps. It was an overdue upgrade, and I decided to do something about it.

The Docker container setup was fairly simple, but the portal didn't launch and threw a lot of errors. I could have used Caddy or Nginx to fix it, but neither was as convenient as Tailscale Serve. My Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W was already a part of the Tailnet. I also had to enable MagicDNS and HTTPS support. After that, the server became accessible via the Tailnet IP on all connected devices. I could even use the app on my phone, which didn't work before. So, it solved two problems at once. For 24/7 uptime, as long as there’s no internet outage, I’ve connected the Raspberry Pi setup and router to outlets with an inverter connection. It needs a few Watts to function, and the server remains accessible even during long power outages.

If you don’t have a home-wide inverter connection, you can use a power bank. Connect the power bank to the Raspberry Pi (and to the router as well), then calculate how long it takes to drain the battery. Then you can use timers to recharge the power bank before a blackout happens, or you can use a smart plug to control the setup wirelessly.

A reliable password manager

If you’re frustrated with rising prices or the security risks of cloud password managers, you can switch to a self-hosted option. It’s not easy, since you have to figure out several things, like uptime, power supply, and backups. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is one of the cheapest things to run a password manager server with minimal maintenance. I use an automated backup feature in the OS to save the whole setup on a USB drive. I also occasionally export vaults and save them to multiple external hard drives.
